summary: Examines the overhead of moving user data through the end-system network path at high speeds, which has limited the use of Internet protocols in demanding settings. It addresses an IP-based copy avoidance solution through Remote Direct Memory Access. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When data arrives on a fast network, the receiving computer has to copy it out of the network card's memory and into the application's memory. Those copies use up the memory bandwidth that the processor needs, so the machine cannot keep up with the link. RFC 4297 explains the problem and points at Remote Direct Memory Access, where the network card writes straight into the application's memory.

questions: why is network data copying slow
why is data copying slow on fast networks
what is rdma over ip problem
subtitle: Why moving data between memory and the network costs more than the bandwidth suggests, and what direct access to remote memory changes.

tldr.problem: On fast links the host, not the network, becomes the limit. Every byte of received data is copied at least twice inside the machine, and that copying, not the link speed, decides how much traffic a server can handle.
tldr.mechanism: The document measures the cost of copying, shows that memory bandwidth rather than processor speed is the scarce resource, and describes Remote Direct Memory Access, where the network adapter places data straight into application buffers without the processor copying it.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement. It does not specify the mechanism itself; the architecture for direct data placement and RDMA over IP is in RFC 4296, its companion document.

facts.label: Processor time on data access
facts.value: From 24% to 15% at 370 Mbits/s with copy avoidance

today: RFC 4297 is an Informational problem statement from December 2005 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets out why copying is expensive and points at Remote Direct Memory Access, but it specifies no mechanism of its own; the architecture for direct data placement and RDMA over the Internet Protocol Suite is in RFC 4296, its companion document.

sections.title: Copying Data, Not Bandwidth, Is the Bottleneck
sections.content:
The document considers the problem of high host processing overhead associated with moving user data to and from the network interface under high speed conditions, often called the I/O bottleneck. More specifically, the source of overhead of interest is data movement operations, that is copying. The throughput of a system may therefore be limited by the overhead of this copying. This is not to be confused with TCP offload, which is not addressed here. High speed means conditions where the network link speed is high relative to the bandwidths of the host processor and memory, and with today's computer systems one Gigabit per second and over is considered high speed.

The cost is mainly a problem for large scale systems. Smaller machines such as rack-mounted PCs and small workstations would benefit from a reduction in copying overhead, but that benefit will mainly arrive over the next few years as they scale the bandwidth they handle. Today it is large machines with high bandwidth feeds, usually multiprocessors and clusters, that are adversely affected: database servers, storage servers, application servers for transaction processing, e-commerce and web serving, content and video distribution, backups, data mining and decision support, and scientific computing. Such servers service many concurrent sessions, which in aggregate are responsible for more than 1 Gbits/s of communication, and the cost of the copying overhead for a given load is the same whether it comes from few sessions or many.

Because of this overhead in current implementations, the TCP/IP protocol stack is not used for high speed transfer. Instead, special purpose network fabrics using a technology generally known as Remote Direct Memory Access have been developed and are widely used. RDMA is a set of mechanisms that allow the network adapter, under control of the application, to steer data directly into and out of application buffers. Examples of such fabrics include Fibre Channel for block storage transfer, the Virtual Interface Architecture for database clusters, and Infiniband, Compaq Servernet and Quadrics for system area networks. These link level technologies limit application scaling in both distance and size, because the number of nodes cannot be arbitrarily large.
sections.plainLanguage: On a fast link the bottleneck moves inside the computer. Each byte that arrives has to be copied between memory areas, and those copies eat the memory bandwidth the processor needs to run the application. So the server cannot keep up with the network it was given.

sections.title: What the Measurements Show
sections.content:
Research and industry data show that copying is responsible for substantial amounts of processing overhead, and that eliminating copies significantly reduces it even in carefully implemented systems. In a 1989 study, the processing overhead of TCP was attributable both to operating system costs such as interrupts, context switches, process management, buffer management and timer management, and to the cost of processing individual bytes, specifically computing the checksum and moving data in memory. Moving data in memory was the more important of the two, and memory bandwidth was the greatest source of limitation. In that data, 64% of the measured microsecond overhead was attributable to data touching operations, and 48% was accounted for by copying.

Several studies report that data touching operations, checksumming and data movement dominate the processing costs for messages longer than 128 bytes, while for smaller messages per-packet overheads dominate. The share due to data touching rises with packet size, because time spent on per-byte operations scales with message size. One study reported per-byte latency costs as a percentage of total networking software costs for a full-size packet, using memory-to-memory TCP tests over networks with three different MTU sizes: 18-25% for 1500 byte Ethernet, 35-50% for 4352 byte FDDI, and 55-65% for 9180 byte ATM. A separate study that separated checksum time from data movement found that for the 1500 byte Ethernet size, 20% of total processing overhead time was attributable to copying, with checksum accounting for 30%.

Eliminating copies has been measured to help substantially. One system that aimed at improving web server performance showed a throughput increase of 43% over an optimised web server and a 137% improvement over an Apache server. Another study, measuring processor utilisation, found that avoiding copies reduced the processor time spent on data access from 24% to 15% at 370 Mbits/s, an absolute improvement of 9%, while total processor utilisation was 35%. When the checksum overhead is removed as well, copy avoidance reduced processor utilisation from 26% to 10%, a 16% absolute reduction and a 160% relative improvement in achievable bandwidth. Since today's network interface hardware commonly offloads the checksum and coalesces interrupts, copying accounts for a relatively larger part of processor utilisation than it once did.

The underlying reason is that memory bandwidth is scarce relative to network bandwidth and processor bandwidth. With copies crossing the bus twice per copy, network processing overhead is high whenever network bandwidth is large compared with processor and memory bandwidth, and the effects are observable at network speeds over 1 Gbits/s. Faster processors do not help if the processor spends most of its time waiting for memory. Between 1980 and 1998 microprocessor performance grew at 60% per year while DRAM access time improved at 10% per year, and the STREAM benchmark data show that from 1985 to 2001 processing performance rose at 50% per year on average while sustainable memory bandwidth rose at 35% per year. Network bandwidth has been increasing about ten-fold roughly every eight years, a 40% per year growth rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurements from the 1980s and 1990s show that moving bytes around in memory costs more than everything else the protocol stack does, and that the share grows with the size of the packet. Removing the copies has been measured to cut processor time and raise throughput sharply.

sections.title: Which Applications Pay the Cost
sections.content:
If a significant portion of the resources on an application machine is consumed by network I/O rather than application processing, it becomes difficult for the application to scale, that is, to handle more clients or offer more services. The applications most affected today are those that store, manage and distribute information: database applications doing transaction processing, e-commerce, web serving, decision support, content distribution, video distribution and backups. Clusters are typically used for this category, because they offer availability and scalability advantages.

These applications typically run in data centres organised into three logical tiers. The first is a set of web servers connecting to the WAN. The second is a set of application servers running the specific applications, usually on more powerful machines. The third is the back-end databases. Physically, the first two tiers are usually combined. When network I/O uses too much memory bandwidth, performance on the paths between tiers suffers, because the high overhead from network-related memory copies diverts system resources from other application processing and can create bottlenecks that limit total system performance.

There is high motivation to maximise the processing capacity of each processor, because scaling by adding processors has drawbacks. Adding processors to a multiprocessor does not necessarily help, because a multiprocessor improves performance only when the memory bus has additional bandwidth to spare, and clustering adds complexity to handling the applications. To scale a cluster or multiprocessor system, interconnect bandwidth must be scaled proportionally, because it governs the performance of communication-intensive parallel applications; if it is too low, adding processors cannot improve system throughput.

Copy avoidance scales a machine upwards by removing at least two-thirds of the bus bandwidth load from the best one-copy implementations on receive, and at least 80% of the bandwidth overhead from two-copy implementations. The measurements in the document compare three servers under simulated wide area conditions: Apache, an optimised server called Flash, and the same server running a zero-copy system called Flash-Lite. Flash-Lite had the best throughput at every number of slow background clients, and the gap grew with the number of clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The servers that pay most are the ones at the centre of a data centre: databases, storage and application servers that receive as much data as they send. The copies take memory bandwidth away from the application, and adding more processors does not help when the memory bus is the limit.

sections.title: Two Ways to Avoid Copies
sections.content:
Two main approaches to eliminating data movement overhead have been investigated. In one, hardware and software changes within a single host reduce processing costs. In the other, memory-to-memory networking exchanges explicit data placement information between hosts so that they can reduce processing costs. The single host approaches range from new hardware and software architectures to new or modified software systems. In the approach based on using a networking protocol to exchange information, the network adapter, under control of the application, places data directly into and out of application buffers, reducing the need for data movement. This is commonly called RDMA, Remote Direct Memory Access.

Copy avoidance confined to the receiving path alone has proven problematic. Research special purpose host adapter systems had good performance and can be seen as precursors for the commercial RDMA-based adapters. In software, many implementations have successfully achieved zero-copy transmit, but few have accomplished zero-copy receive, and those that have impose strict alignment and no-touch requirements on the application, which greatly reduces portability and usefulness. Software optimisations of the single host kind have also been complex, fragile, extremely interdependent with other system parameters, and often of only marginal improvement. The Solaris zero-copy TCP work, which relies on page remapping, is highly interdependent with other systems such as the file system, and its optimisations are specific to particular architectures, so they must be re-crafted for each variation.

Experience with memory-to-memory systems that permit RDMA has been satisfactory: performance has been good and there have been no system or networking difficulties. RDMA is a single solution. Once implemented it can be used with any operating system and machine architecture, and it does not need to be revised when either changes. With RDMA, application I/O buffers are mapped directly, and the authorised peer may access them without additional processing overhead. When RDMA is implemented in hardware, arbitrary data movement can be performed without involving the host processor at all.
sections.plainLanguage: You can remove copies by changing one machine, or by letting the two machines share memory across the network. The first is fragile and tied to the operating system. The second works with any machine and needs no changes when the hardware changes.

sections.title: Direct Data Placement and RDMA Semantics
sections.content:
An RDMA solution can usefully be viewed as two distinct components: direct data placement, abbreviated DDP, and RDMA semantics. They are distinct in purpose and in practice, and may be implemented as separate protocols.

The more fundamental of the two is the direct data placement facility. This is the means by which memory is exposed to the remote peer in an appropriate fashion, and the means by which the peer may access it, for instance reading and writing it.

The RDMA control functions are semantically layered on top of direct data placement. They include operations that provide control features such as connection and termination, the ordering of operations and the signalling of their completions. A send facility is provided as well.

Historically both aspects taken together have been referred to as RDMA. The facilities of direct data placement are useful in themselves and may be employed by other upper layer protocols to facilitate data transfer, so it is often useful to refer to DDP as the data placement functionality and RDMA as the control aspect. The document points to RFC 4296, its companion, which develops an architecture for DDP and RDMA atop the Internet Protocol Suite.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote direct memory access has two parts. The first exposes a region of memory so the other machine can read or write it. The second is the set of rules for starting a connection, ordering the operations and reporting when they finish.

sections.title: What Copy Avoidance Does to Security
sections.content:
Solutions to the problem of reducing copying overhead in high bandwidth transfers may introduce new security concerns, and any proposed solution must be analysed for vulnerabilities and have them addressed. Potential weaknesses include resource issues that might lead to denial of service attacks, overwrites and other concurrent operations, the ordering of completions required by the RDMA protocol, and the granularity of transfer.

Layered atop Internet transport protocols, the RDMA protocols will gain leverage from and must permit integration with Internet security standards such as IPsec and TLS, although there may be implementation ramifications for some approaches because of the copy avoidance itself. IPsec, which secures the connection on a packet-by-packet basis, seems a natural fit, because RDMA enables an implementation to avoid buffering, and it is preferable to perform all applicable security protection before each segment is processed by the transport and RDMA layers. The TLS record protocol, on the other hand, is layered on top of reliable transports and cannot provide that assurance until an entire record is available, which may require buffering and assembling several messages. That defers RDMA processing and introduces overheads RDMA is designed to avoid, so TLS is viewed as potentially a less natural fit.

It is necessary to guarantee confidentiality, integrity and authentication on an RDMA communications channel, but these properties cannot defend against attacks from properly authenticated peers that might be malicious, compromised or buggy. An RDMA peer should not be able to read or write memory regions without prior consent, and it must not be possible to evade memory consistency checks at the recipient: the design must allow the recipient to rely on consistent memory contents by explicitly controlling peer access to memory regions at appropriate times. Peer connections that do not pass authentication and authorisation checks by upper layers must not be permitted to begin processing in RDMA mode, and once associated, peer accesses to memory regions must be authenticated and subject to authorisation checks in the context of the association and connection, before any transfer operation or data is accessed. These region protections must be under strict application control, because remote access to local memory by a network peer can be exported globally in the Internet context.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting another machine write straight into your memory removes the buffer that security software usually inspects, so the protection has to happen earlier in the path. The rules also have to stop an authenticated but malicious peer from reading or writing memory it was not given.

items.title: Change one host
items.text: New hardware, architecture or software inside a single machine. Zero-copy transmit works, but zero-copy receive is rare and imposes strict alignment and no-touch rules on the application.

items.title: Memory-to-memory networking
items.text: The network adapter places data directly into and out of application buffers under application control. It works with any operating system and machine architecture.

items.title: Why the second approach is preferred
items.text: Single host optimisations are complex, fragile, interdependent with other system parameters, and often of only marginal improvement.
